title: Luke 8:40–56
context: Jairus pleads for his dying daughter while a woman with twelve years of bleeding seeks healing amid the crowd. Jesus brings the woman’s restoration into the open and answers the child’s death with a life-giving command, calling for trust without turning these particular miracles into a universal promise of immediate healing.

verses.text: When Jesus returned, the multitude welcomed him, for they were all waiting for him.
verses.arminianNotes: The returning crowd welcomes Jesus, unlike those across the lake. Arminian readers see different responses without assuming every welcoming person already has mature faith.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise distinguish welcome from a full account of spiritual condition. The scene moves toward two desperate needs within the waiting multitude.

verses.text: Behold, a man named Jairus came. He was a ruler of the synagogue. He fell down at Jesus’ feet and begged him to come into his house,
verses.arminianNotes: Jairus, a synagogue ruler, falls before Jesus to plead for help. Arminian readers see status yielding to dependence when his daughter’s life is threatened.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise recognize humble petition rather than confidence in office. Social standing supplies no substitute for Christ’s mercy.

verses.text: for he had an only born daughter, about twelve years of age, and she was dying. But as he went, the multitudes pressed against him.
verses.arminianNotes: Jairus’s only daughter is dying as the crowd slows the journey. Arminian readers see urgency and the painful tension when another need interrupts.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise attend to this child and the pressure of delay. The WEB’s only born means his one and only daughter, not a special spiritual rank.

verses.text: A woman who had a flow of blood for twelve years, who had spent all her living on physicians and could not be healed by any,
verses.arminianNotes: Long bleeding and exhausted resources reveal the woman’s need. Arminian readers retain the WEB’s statement about physicians without making it a condemnation of medical care.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see failed remedies highlighting helplessness, not a rule against treatment. The selected source prints the full expenditure clause, so it is retained rather than shortened.

verses.text: came behind him and touched the fringe of his cloak. Immediately the flow of her blood stopped.
verses.arminianNotes: Her touch is followed by immediate healing. Arminian readers see trusting approach to Jesus, not a magical garment; fringe or tassel concerns clothing terminology.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise locate power in Christ. Contact occasions this gift; it is not a technique obliging God to cure every illness in the same way.

verses.text: Jesus said, “Who touched me?” When all denied it, Peter and those with him said, “Master, the multitudes press and jostle you, and you say, ‘Who touched me?’”
verses.arminianNotes: Jesus distinguishes a particular touch from the crowd’s jostling. Arminian readers see a hidden encounter brought into personal recognition rather than left anonymous.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise distinguish proximity from this encounter. The WEB includes Peter and those with him and the repeated question; both are retained as printed.

verses.text: But Jesus said, “Someone did touch me, for I perceived that power has gone out of me.”
verses.arminianNotes: Jesus identifies the touch through power going out from him. Arminian readers see personal ministry, not an impersonal cure obtained from an object.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise affirm that power belongs to Jesus. The statement should not become a theory that his strength is depleted or that he heals involuntarily.

verses.text: When the woman saw that she was not hidden, she came trembling; and falling down before him declared to him in the presence of all the people the reason why she had touched him, and how she was healed immediately.
verses.arminianNotes: The woman trembles and publicly tells what happened. Arminian readers see vulnerable honesty met by reassurance rather than condemnation for approaching in need.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise recognize movement from hidden suffering to acknowledged restoration. Her confession reports the cure; it does not purchase a healing already received.

verses.text: He said to her, “Daughter, cheer up. Your faith has made you well. Go in peace.”
verses.arminianNotes: Jesus calls her daughter and sends her in peace. Arminian readers see faith as receptive trust, not a meritorious force, and healing as Christ’s gift.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise emphasize Christ as the power faith receives. Neither tradition should turn this woman’s assurance into an accusation that every unhealed person lacks faith.

verses.text: While he still spoke, one from the ruler of the synagogue’s house came, saying to him, “Your daughter is dead. Don’t trouble the Teacher.”
verses.arminianNotes: The report of death makes Jairus’s request appear too late. Arminian readers see the severity of the interruption without treating the messenger’s conclusion as Jesus’ limit.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the message’s ordinary human finality. Jesus confronts that conclusion without denying the reality of the family’s bereavement.

verses.text: But Jesus hearing it, answered him, “Don’t be afraid. Only believe, and she will be healed.”
verses.arminianNotes: Jesus calls Jairus from fear to faith with a particular promise about his daughter. Arminian readers see trust sustained amid devastating news by Christ’s word.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise ground hope in that promise, not faith as an independent power. This assurance is not a universal guarantee that every dying child will recover now.

verses.text: When he came to the house, he didn’t allow anyone to enter in, except Peter, John, James, the father of the child, and her mother.
verses.arminianNotes: Jesus limits entry to three disciples and the parents. Arminian readers see a restrained, personal setting rather than a performance designed for publicity.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note his control of the encounter. The witnesses serve this event; the text does not explain every reason for naming these three disciples.

verses.text: All were weeping and mourning her, but he said, “Don’t weep. She isn’t dead, but sleeping.”
verses.arminianNotes: Jesus describes death as sleep in view of his coming action. Arminian readers read this with the death report, not as denial that the girl died.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise understand death as not final before Christ’s life-giving authority. His reassurance rests on what he will do, not on minimizing grief.

verses.text: They were ridiculing him, knowing that she was dead.
verses.arminianNotes: The mourners ridicule Jesus because they know the girl died. Arminian readers see unbelief made explicit while the account confirms the reality of death.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note that restoration does not depend on the crowd’s confidence. Their mockery cannot overturn Christ’s authority, though it remains an inappropriate response.

verses.text: But he put them all outside, and taking her by the hand, he called, saying, “Child, arise!”
verses.arminianNotes: Jesus takes the child’s hand and commands her to arise. Arminian readers see tenderness joined to authority the child cannot supply for herself.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise emphasize the effective, life-giving word. Both affirm the miracle without using it alone to settle every disputed question about the order of salvation.

verses.text: Her spirit returned, and she rose up immediately. He commanded that something be given to her to eat.
verses.arminianNotes: Her spirit returns, she rises, and Jesus orders food. Arminian readers see bodily restoration and practical care joined, not an appearance without ordinary needs.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise recognize real, immediate restoration. Concern for nourishment preserves the child’s humanity rather than treating her as an exhibit.

verses.text: Her parents were amazed, but he commanded them to tell no one what had been done.
verses.arminianNotes: The parents are astonished but told not to publicize the event. Arminian readers see obedience differing here from the former demoniac’s commission.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise resist inventing a complete explanation for silence. The contrast with verse 39 shows that Christ’s particular command governs response, not a uniform publicity rule.
